newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serb PM says privatisation should aid bank reform.
newsitem.headline: Serb PM says privatisation should aid bank reform.

text.p: Serbia is determined to take advantage of privatisation to overhaul its oversized, capital-starved and inefficient banking sector, Serbian Prime Minister Mirko Marjanovic told Reuters.
"Restructuring of companies, partially through their privatisation, will help speed up the bank overhaul programme," Marjanovic told Reuters in written answers to questions.
Banks themselves are not up for privatisation but the government has drafted a programme to transform ownership of most other companies within two years.
"We expect banks to take steps on their own to downsize, restructure, increase efficiency, secure deposits, extend credits," he said.

Yugoslavia has more than 100 banks, all owned by state-run shareholder companies. Nearly half of them are "old" banks while the rest emerged since the early 1990s after the former Balkan federation broke up.
The old banks are burdened with over $4 billion in debt derived from individual hard currency savings frozen since 1991.

These are acknowledged as a public liability and Serbia has already called on the federal government to prepare a programme to release the frozen savings. It is also seeking a rescheduling of Yugoslavia's external debt, estimated by independent economists at close to $10 billion.

"The state must define its obligations to hard currency depositors and ways to service the debt. The federal government has just prepared a draft law to tackle this very sensitive issue," Marjanovic said.
He said it was also finalising legal solutions aimed at restoring confidence in the local financial system.

The savings freeze and a collapse of two pyramid savings schemes in 1993 buried confidence in Yugoslav banks. According to an independent study, Yugoslavs held on the average just 11 dinars ($1.9) in savings accounts in 1996.

"The runaway inflation in 1991-1993 period, before this government took office, had devastated companies' and banks' accounts, made extended credits worthless and terribly intensified the problem of hard currency savings," Marjanovic said.
In 1993, Yugoslavia struggled with hyper-inflation running at 60 percent a day.
The Prime Minister said bank rehabilitation must begin with facing those financial facts, no matter how bitter they may be.
He said both banks and companies needed to operate under stricter financial discipline than they had been used to.
Another important precondition for creating a healthy banking sector was to clarify and define ownership relations between banks and debtors companies to whom they had made loans.
Marjanovic said Yugoslavia would benefit from the presence of foreign banks to introduce international standards and know-how and to bring in foreign capital.
Meanwhile, many Yugoslav banks have not yet restored international payment operations.

"Normal international payment operations still do not exist while substantial funds of our companies and banks remain frozen abroad. Over the last several years, our economy and banks could not rely on a single cent of external financial help," Marjanovic said.
He offered reassurance to those who feared mergers were creating monopolies in the banking sector.

"Banking mergers will be conducted only in order to give banks more financial strength and...will not hinder many competitive banks which know how to behave in a market economy," -- Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 311 4254
